topic: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
parentTitle: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
title: Dysphagia and IDDSI levels
blurb: Spot the signs of dysphagia, refer to speech and language therapy, and serve food and drink at exactly the IDDSI level in the person's plan.
question: Daisy, 44, has a severe learning disability and cerebral palsy. Her carers say she coughs during drinks, her voice sounds 'gurgly' after meals and she has had two chest infections this winter. What should the nurse do, and how will her drinks be described if they need changing?

teach.body: Dysphagia is the medical term for swallowing problems: difficulty in any stage of eating, drinking and swallowing. People with learning disabilities are more likely to have it, and the signs are often missed, especially when the person cannot describe them. It can cause choking, aspiration pneumonia, dehydration, malnutrition and constipation. In plain English: food or drink may be going the wrong way, and nobody may notice until the person is ill.
teach.cite: PHE, Dysphagia in people with learning difficulties (2016)

head: Sign
What it may mean
rows: Wet or gurgly voice after eating
teach.caption: Ask family and support staff: they see the person eat every day.

teach.h: Refer, then follow the plan exactly
teach.body: Anyone with signs of dysphagia is referred to speech and language therapy (SLT). The SLT assesses the swallow, sometimes with videofluoroscopy or FEES, and writes an eating and drinking plan: texture, equipment, position, pacing and environment. Everyone who supports the person follows it in every setting, including hospital. PHE notes supporters stick well to textures and equipment but often forget pacing and prompting, so train on the reasons, not just the rules.

teach.caption: Drinks use levels 0-4; foods use levels 3-7. Levels 3 and 4 have both a drink and a food name.

head: Test
Used for
Key point
teach.caption: Level 6 adult pieces are about 15 mm, soft enough to mash with a fork.

teach.h: Flow test: mL left after 10 seconds
teach.caption: Fill a 10 mL slip-tip syringe, let it flow for 10 seconds, read what is left.

items: Check the plan: IDDSI level for food and drink, equipment, position.
Sit the person as upright as possible, head in midline, as the plan and postural care advise.
Reduce distractions: noise, heat, light and people moving about.
Pace as the plan says; wait for each swallow; never rush.
Stay upright after the meal; give mouth care.
Record intake and any coughing, and report changes to SLT.

teach.body: Coughing on drinks, a wet voice and repeated chest infections point to dysphagia with aspiration. The nurse refers Daisy to SLT, and meanwhile ensures she sits upright and is not rushed. The SLT recommends IDDSI level 2 mildly thick drinks and a slow pace. The nurse teaches staff to check a drink with the flow test (4-8 mL left after 10 seconds) and asks the GP to review her medicines, as some can worsen swallowing.

teach.text: Two classic mistakes: thickening drinks 'to be safe' without an SLT assessment, and mixing up levels 3 and 4, which have different names for drinks (moderately thick, extremely thick) and foods (liquidised, pureed). Also, a person with capacity may choose not to follow their plan: support them to reduce risk rather than overriding their decision.

items: Signs: coughing, wet voice, chest infections, long meals, weight loss, refusal.
Refer to SLT; follow the eating and drinking plan in every setting.
Flow test: 10 mL syringe, 10 seconds; level 2 leaves 4-8 mL.
Upright, unhurried, low-distraction meals; review medicines that affect swallowing.

summary: You can now recognise the signs of dysphagia and refer to speech and language therapy. You can name the eight IDDSI levels, check drinks with the flow test, and support safe, paced, upright mealtimes as the plan sets out.

A.q: Tom, 37, has a learning disability and dysphagia. His new SLT plan says IDDSI level 2 drinks. Which drink description matches this level?
options: Slightly thick
Moderately thick
Mildly thick
Extremely thick
A.why: IDDSI drinks: 0 thin, 1 slightly thick, 2 mildly thick, 3 moderately thick, 4 extremely thick.

A.q: Asif, 52, has a learning disability. His SLT recommends an IDDSI level 5 diet. What does this level mean?
options: Minced and moist food with small soft lumps
Smooth pureed food that has no lumps
Soft and bite-sized pieces of about 15 mm each
Regular food that is easy to chew
A.why: IDDSI level 5 is minced and moist: small soft lumps about 4 mm for adults, the size of the gaps between fork prongs.

whyNot.2: Soft and bite-sized pieces are level 6.
whyNot.3: Regular and easy to chew foods are level 7.

A.q: A carer asks how many levels there are in the IDDSI framework and which apply to drinks. Which answer is correct?
options: Seven levels; drinks use levels 1 to 4
Eight levels; drinks use levels 0 to 4
Eight levels; drinks use levels 0 to 3
Ten levels; drinks use levels 0 to 5
A.why: IDDSI has 8 levels numbered 0 to 7: drinks 0 to 4 and foods 3 to 7.

whyNot.0: There are eight levels, starting at 0.
whyNot.3: There are eight levels, not ten.

B.q: Daisy, 44, has a severe learning disability and cerebral palsy. She coughs during drinks, her voice sounds wet after meals and she has had two chest infections this winter. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Thicken all her drinks to level 4 straight away
Refer her to speech and language therapy
Change her to a pureed diet for one month
Ask her GP for antibiotics to keep at home
B.why: Coughing, a wet voice and recurrent chest infections suggest dysphagia with aspiration. She needs SLT assessment; changes to texture are made on SLT advice.

whyNot.0: Thickening without assessment may be wrong for her and can cause dehydration.
whyNot.2: Texture changes need SLT assessment first.
whyNot.3: Treating infections does not address the cause.

B.q: Jamie, 41, has an SLT plan for IDDSI level 1 drinks. A new carer has made a drink and is unsure if it is the right thickness. How should it be checked?
options: With the fork drip test
With the spoon tilt test
With the fork pressure test
With the IDDSI flow test
B.why: The IDDSI flow test uses a 10 mL slip-tip syringe for 10 seconds: level 1 slightly thick leaves 1 to 4 mL.

whyNot.0: The fork drip test is for foods at levels 3 to 5.
whyNot.1: The spoon tilt test checks stickiness and cohesion of foods.
whyNot.2: The fork pressure test is for foods from level 4 upwards.

B.q: Mia, 30, has a profound learning disability and an SLT eating and drinking plan. Which position best protects her airway at mealtimes?
options: Sitting upright with her head in midline
Reclined at 30 degrees with her head back
Lying on her side with her knees bent
Reclined fully with her head on a pillow
B.why: Sitting as upright as possible with the head in midline protects the airway during swallowing; her SLT plan and postural care plan give the detail.

whyNot.1: Reclining with the head tilted back opens the airway to aspiration.
whyNot.2: Side-lying is a recovery position, not a safe eating posture for most people.

C.q: Chris, 39, has a learning disability and an SLT plan for IDDSI level 6 food. In hospital he is served a steak meal cut into small pieces. What should the nurse do?
options: Cut the steak into smaller pieces before serving
Serve it, since the pieces look about 15 mm
Return it and order a meal that matches level 6
Let Chris choose whether to eat it or the dessert
C.why: Level 6 food must be soft and tender, in about 15 mm pieces that can be mashed with a fork. Steak cannot meet this by cutting, so a meal matching the level is needed.

whyNot.0: Smaller pieces do not make tough meat soft enough for level 6.
whyNot.1: Size is only one part; texture must pass the fork pressure test.
whyNot.3: Offering an unsafe meal as a choice does not follow his plan.

C.q: Ethan, 35, has a learning disability and an SLT plan for level 2 drinks. At a family party he wants a thin fizzy drink. He has been assessed as having capacity to decide and understands the risk. What should the nurse do?
options: Thicken the drink without telling him
Remove the drink and remind him about his SLT plan
Support his choice and help him drink safely
Ask his family to decide for him on the day
C.why: Ethan has capacity for this decision, so under MCA 2005 s1(4) he may make an unwise choice. The nurse supports him to reduce risk (upright, small sips, slow pace) and records the discussion.

whyNot.0: Covertly altering his drink overrides a capacitous decision.
whyNot.1: Removing the drink ignores his right to decide.
whyNot.3: Family cannot decide for an adult with capacity.

C.q: Isla, 26, has a learning disability and dysphagia. She has lost 4 kg in two months, meals now take over an hour, and she pushes food away. Her SLT plan is a year old. What is the best action?
options: Give her nutritional supplements and recheck her weight next month
Change her to IDDSI level 4 pureed meals from today
Offer smaller meals more often and keep the same plan
Refer back to SLT and a dietitian for an urgent review
C.why: Weight loss, long meals and food refusal suggest her swallowing has changed and the plan no longer meets her needs. SLT and dietetic review are needed; PHE also highlights nutritional assessment.

whyNot.0: Supplements without review may be unsafe and miss a worsening swallow.
whyNot.1: Changing texture without SLT assessment may be wrong for her.
whyNot.2: Keeping an out-of-date plan ignores clear signs of change.

reteach.title: Numbers that keep people safe
reteach.question: How can a number on a care plan prevent a death?

blocks.body: Before IDDSI, 'soft' or 'thick' meant different things to different people. IDDSI gives every texture a number and a name and a simple test, so a level 2 drink is the same in a care home, a hospital and a family kitchen. The number only protects the person if it is followed exactly and tested.

blocks.text: Never change a level yourself: if the person seems to be struggling, stop, keep them upright and ask SLT to reassess.

explain.body: Coughing or choking, a wet voice, chest infections, long meals, weight loss and refusing food are all signs. Family and support staff are key observers.

test.q: Which finding most strongly suggests a person has dysphagia?
options: A preference for sweet foods
A wet, gurgly voice after drinks
Eating faster than other people at meals
Asking for second helpings
test.why: A wet or gurgly voice after drinking suggests residue near the airway, a sign of dysphagia.

whyNot.0: Food preference is not a swallowing sign.
whyNot.2: Fast eating is a risk, not itself a sign of dysphagia.
whyNot.3: A good appetite does not suggest swallowing difficulty.

explain.body: Drinks: 0 thin, 1 slightly thick, 2 mildly thick, 3 moderately thick, 4 extremely thick. Foods: 3 liquidised, 4 pureed, 5 minced and moist, 6 soft and bite-sized, 7 regular.

test.q: Which IDDSI food level is soft and bite-sized?
options: Level 4
Level 5
Level 6
Level 7
test.why: Level 6 is soft and bite-sized, adult pieces about 15 mm.

explain.body: 10 mL slip-tip syringe, flow for 10 seconds. Under 1 mL left: thin (0). 1-4 mL: slightly thick (1). 4-8 mL: mildly thick (2). More than 8 mL: moderately thick (3).

test.q: A drink leaves 6 mL in the syringe after the 10-second flow test. Which level is it?
options: Level 0 thin
Level 1 slightly thick
Level 3 moderately thick
Level 2 mildly thick
test.why: 4 to 8 mL remaining is level 2, mildly thick.

whyNot.2: Moderately thick leaves more than 8 mL.

explain.body: Upright posture, minimal distractions, pacing and mouth care. PHE warns that medicines, particularly antipsychotics, can contribute to or cause dysphagia, so review them; crushing tablets can change how they work, so ask a pharmacist.

test.q: A man with dysphagia struggles to swallow tablets. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the prescriber or pharmacist about another form
Crush all his tablets into his pureed food
Omit the tablets he cannot swallow easily
Give each tablet separately with a thin drink of water
test.why: PHE guidance: alternatives such as liquids, patches or suppositories may be needed, and crushing can affect how a medicine works; get prescriber or pharmacist advice.

whyNot.1: Crushing can alter release and some medicines must not be crushed.
whyNot.2: Omitting medicines without review risks harm.
whyNot.3: Thin drinks may be unsafe for someone with dysphagia.
